title: DayQuil and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Each Ingredient Explained
excerpt: Is it safe to drink on DayQuil? How acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, and phenylephrine each interact with alcohol, why DayQuil has no alcohol (NyQuil does), and how long to wait.
metaDescription: Can you drink on DayQuil? How its acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, and phenylephrine interact with alcohol, how long to wait, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's best not to drink while you're taking DayQuil. One drink with one dose is unlikely to cause a crisis in a healthy adult, but the combination stacks up in ways people don't expect. The biggest concern is the **acetaminophen** (the active ingredient in Tylenol) that's in every standard DayQuil Cold & Flu dose. Acetaminophen and alcohol both put work on your liver, and the risk climbs fast if you drink heavily, take more than the label allows, or take DayQuil together with another product that also contains acetaminophen. The other two ingredients matter less, but they aren't nothing: **dextromethorphan** can add to alcohol's dizziness and drowsiness, and **phenylephrine** plus alcohol can nudge up your heart rate. And you're sick, which is exactly when your body needs alcohol least.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink while DayQuil is in your system, and don't take DayQuil to treat a hangover. Never take Tylenol or any other acetaminophen product on top of DayQuil. If you drink 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using DayQuil at all, because the label says so. If you think you or someone else took too much acetaminophen, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away, even if they feel fine.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the information printed on US over-the-counter labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the medicines you take. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining DayQuil and alcohol if** you drink heavily most days, have liver disease, high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate, or if you take an antidepressant or any prescription medicine. **Get help now (call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or 911 in an emergency) if** you may have taken more than the labeled dose, or you notice nausea, vomiting, pain under your right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, confusion, a racing or pounding heartbeat, severe dizziness, or trouble breathing.

## What's Actually in DayQuil

DayQuil is a brand of Vicks, and the name covers several products. The most common one, **Vicks DayQuil Cold & Flu**, comes as LiquiCaps and as a liquid. Each standard dose combines three active ingredients:

| Ingredient | What it does | Per 2 LiquiCaps (one adult dose) |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaminophen | Pain reliever and fever reducer | 650 mg |
| Dextromethorphan HBr | Cough suppressant | 20 mg |
| Phenylephrine HCl | Nasal decongestant | 10 mg |

The liquid version delivers the same amounts in a 30 mL dose. The adult label says to take a dose every 4 hours and **no more than 4 doses in 24 hours**, which works out to 2,600 mg of acetaminophen a day from DayQuil alone.

Other versions add or change ingredients. **DayQuil Severe** adds guaifenesin, an expectorant that loosens mucus. Some cough-only and sinus products in the Vicks line use different combinations. Store brands sold as "daytime cold and flu" usually copy the same three-ingredient formula. The point is simple: **read the Drug Facts box on the exact package you own.** Everything below is about the standard formula, and you should check whether yours matches.

Notice what's *not* in DayQuil: there's no sedating antihistamine. That's the main difference from NyQuil, and it's why DayQuil is sold as "non-drowsy." It matters a lot when alcohol enters the picture, which we'll come back to.

## Ingredient 1: Acetaminophen and Alcohol (the Real Safety Issue)

Acetaminophen is the ingredient that makes DayQuil and alcohol a genuine safety question rather than just a bad idea. It's also the ingredient people forget is there.

### How the liver handles acetaminophen

Your liver clears most of each acetaminophen dose through safe routes that attach it to other molecules so it can leave in your urine. A smaller share goes through a liver enzyme called **CYP2E1**, which turns it into a toxic by-product called **NAPQI**. Normally, an antioxidant your liver keeps on hand, **glutathione**, neutralizes NAPQI right away.

Trouble starts when NAPQI is made faster than glutathione can clear it. Alcohol can push both sides of that balance in the wrong direction:

- **Regular heavy drinking increases CYP2E1.** The same enzyme helps break down alcohol, so a liver that sees a lot of alcohol makes more of it. More enzyme means more of each acetaminophen dose goes down the toxic route.
- **Heavy drinking and poor eating lower glutathione.** Long-term drinking, skipped meals, and being sick with a poor appetite all tend to reduce the liver's clean-up capacity.

This is why the risk is concentrated in people who drink heavily on a regular basis and in anyone who takes too much acetaminophen. It's also why being sick matters: if you've barely eaten for two days because of a cold or flu, your glutathione reserve may be lower than usual. Our [full guide to Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) goes deeper into the liver chemistry, safe limits, and warning signs.

### What the label and the research say

Acetaminophen overdose is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States. Data from the US Acute Liver Failure Study Group have attributed roughly half of cases to acetaminophen, and a large share of those were accidental: people taking a little too much over several days, often from more than one product, sometimes alongside alcohol.

Because of that, the US Food and Drug Administration has required a liver warning on over-the-counter acetaminophen products since 2009. The DayQuil label carries it. In plain words, it warns that **severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the maximum daily doses, take it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product.**

### The hidden-acetaminophen trap

The most realistic way someone gets into trouble with DayQuil isn't one drink. It's stacking:

- Taking DayQuil during the day, then **NyQuil at night**. Standard NyQuil Cold & Flu also contains acetaminophen, so both count toward the same daily total.
- Taking DayQuil and then reaching for **Tylenol** for a headache or fever, not realizing DayQuil already has 650 mg per dose.
- Using DayQuil alongside another cold product, such as some versions of Theraflu, Mucinex, or Alka-Seltzer Plus, many of which also contain acetaminophen.
- Having a few drinks, waking up with a hangover headache, and taking Tylenol "for the headache" and DayQuil "for the cold" in the same morning.

Each of these can push your total acetaminophen past the label's limit without you noticing, and adding alcohol on top of that is the scenario the label warning was written for. **Count acetaminophen from every product, every day.** On US labels it may be listed as "acetaminophen" or "APAP"; outside North America the same drug is called paracetamol.

## Ingredient 2: Dextromethorphan and Alcohol

Dextromethorphan, often shortened to DXM, is the cough suppressant in DayQuil. At the labeled dose it works on the cough center in the brain, and for most people it causes few side effects. The issue with alcohol is that both affect the brain, and their effects can add up.

### What happens when you combine them

At normal DayQuil doses, the most likely effects of adding alcohol are **more dizziness, more drowsiness, and worse coordination and judgment** than you'd get from alcohol alone. DayQuil's "non-drowsy" label describes the lack of an antihistamine. It doesn't mean dextromethorphan can't make you lightheaded, and some people do feel drowsy or dizzy on it, especially combined with alcohol. That's a real concern if you plan to drive, bike, or do anything where reaction time matters.

### Why DXM is not the same for everyone

Your body breaks down dextromethorphan mainly with a liver enzyme called **CYP2D6**. People inherit different versions of this enzyme. A minority of people are "poor metabolizers," and in them dextromethorphan can stay in the body for much longer than in the typical person, so its effects last longer and build up more with repeat doses. You usually have no way of knowing which group you're in without testing. That's one reason a fixed rule like "wait two hours" doesn't work for everyone.

### The high-dose and drug-interaction risks

Two situations make dextromethorphan plus alcohol genuinely dangerous:

- **Taking more than the label dose.** At high doses, dextromethorphan acts very differently, producing confusion, agitation, hallucinations, a fast heart rate, and in serious cases dangerous breathing and heart problems. Alcohol adds to the sedation and impairment. Taking a lot of DayQuil to get that effect is also a direct route to acetaminophen poisoning, because you swallow far more acetaminophen at the same time.
- **Combining it with certain antidepressants.** The DayQuil label says not to use it if you take an MAOI (a type of antidepressant) or within 2 weeks of stopping one. Dextromethorphan also has a recognized, though uncommon, risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with other drugs that raise serotonin, including some SSRIs and SNRIs. Alcohol doesn't cause serotonin syndrome, but people on antidepressants are often also advised to limit alcohol. If you take any antidepressant, ask a pharmacist before using DayQuil, with or without a drink.

## Ingredient 3: Phenylephrine and Alcohol

Phenylephrine is the decongestant in DayQuil. It narrows blood vessels, the idea being that this shrinks swollen tissue in your nose.

### The interaction with alcohol is modest

There's no well-known dangerous chemical interaction between phenylephrine and alcohol. The concerns are about effects that point the same direction:

- **Heart rate and blood pressure.** Phenylephrine can raise blood pressure, and drinking, especially heavy drinking, can raise heart rate and, over time, blood pressure. For a healthy adult at the labeled dose, the combination is unlikely to matter much. For someone with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart rhythm problem, it's worth avoiding. The label already tells people with these conditions to ask a doctor before use.
- **Feeling jittery or unwell.** Some people feel restless or nervous on decongestants. Add alcohol, a fever, and poor sleep, and you can end up feeling worse rather than better.

### Does the phenylephrine in DayQuil even work?

This is worth knowing. In September 2023, an FDA advisory committee concluded that **oral phenylephrine at the standard dose is not effective as a nasal decongestant**, largely because so little of a swallowed dose reaches the bloodstream in active form. In November 2024, the FDA proposed removing oral phenylephrine from the list of approved over-the-counter decongestant ingredients. As of this writing, products containing it are still on shelves while that process plays out, and some manufacturers have begun reformulating. The practical takeaway: if stuffiness is your main symptom, the phenylephrine in DayQuil may not be doing much for you, and a pharmacist can suggest alternatives that suit your health.

## Does DayQuil Have Alcohol in It?

**No, the standard DayQuil Cold & Flu formulas don't list alcohol as an ingredient.** This question comes up a lot because people mix up DayQuil and NyQuil, and NyQuil is the one with the alcohol reputation.

Here's how the two differ:

- **DayQuil** (daytime): acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, and phenylephrine. No sedating antihistamine. The standard liquid and LiquiCaps don't contain alcohol.
- **NyQuil** (nighttime): acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, and **doxylamine**, a sedating antihistamine that helps you sleep. The original **NyQuil liquid lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient**. Vicks also sells alcohol-free NyQuil versions, and NyQuil LiquiCaps don't contain the alcohol the liquid does.

Formulas change over time and differ between countries and store brands, so if avoiding alcohol completely matters to you (for example, you're in recovery, pregnant, or take a medicine that reacts with alcohol), check the "inactive ingredients" list on the package. Pharmacists can also point you to alcohol-free options.

### Why NyQuil and alcohol is the riskier pair

If you're comparing the two, NyQuil plus alcohol is the more dangerous combination. Doxylamine and alcohol are both sedating, and together they can cause heavy drowsiness, poor coordination, and in larger amounts slowed breathing. NyQuil still contains acetaminophen, so it shares DayQuil's liver concern too. If you've been drinking, don't take NyQuil to help you sleep.

## Can You Drink on DayQuil? What About Timing?

There's no official waiting period printed on the label, and there's no single number that's right for everyone. What we can do is explain how long each piece tends to stay active and give a cautious, practical approach.

### How long DayQuil stays in your system

DayQuil is dosed every 4 hours because that's roughly how long its effects last. The ingredients are cleared at different speeds: acetaminophen and phenylephrine are typically cleared within several hours in a healthy adult, while dextromethorphan can last much longer in people whose bodies break it down slowly. Sources also differ on exact figures, so treat any precise number you see online with caution.

### If you've taken DayQuil and want a drink

- **The safest choice is to skip alcohol while you're sick and taking cold medicine.** Alcohol won't help you recover, and it adds risk.
- If you do decide to drink, a cautious approach is to wait until at least the end of the 4-hour dosing window, and ideally longer, and to keep it to one drink. Don't take another DayQuil dose while you're drinking.
- If you drink 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, the label says to ask a doctor before using DayQuil at all. That's not a timing issue, it's a "check first" issue.

### If you've been drinking and want to take DayQuil

- **Wait until the alcohol has cleared.** The body processes roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies a lot with body size, sex, food, and drinking history. After a heavy night, that can mean waiting well into the next day.
- **Eat first** and drink water.
- **Take one standard dose, not extra,** and don't take Tylenol or any other acetaminophen product on top of it.
- If you drank heavily, consider whether you need DayQuil's acetaminophen at all. If your main problem is congestion or cough, a single-ingredient product without acetaminophen may make more sense. A pharmacist can help you choose.

## Don't Use DayQuil as a Hangover Cure

It's tempting to think DayQuil is an all-in-one fix for a rough morning: it has a pain reliever for the headache and something for the "stuffy" feeling. But it isn't designed for hangovers, and using it that way is one of the more common routes to taking acetaminophen right after alcohol.

- A hangover isn't a cold. Cough suppressants and decongestants don't treat what's driving a hangover, which involves dehydration, disrupted sleep, inflammation, and the after-effects of the body breaking down alcohol.
- The morning after heavy drinking is a poor time for the liver to take on acetaminophen, especially if you haven't eaten.
- If you also take Tylenol or a "hangover" pain reliever that contains acetaminophen, you're stacking doses.

If you need help with a hangover headache, see our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025), which covers what works and the trade-offs of each painkiller. If an upset stomach is the issue, our article on [Pepto Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) explains when that is and isn't a good idea.

## Why Drinking When You Have a Cold or Flu Is a Bad Idea Anyway

Even if DayQuil weren't in the picture, alcohol and a respiratory infection are a poor match:

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol increases urine output. Fever, sweating, and a runny nose already cost you fluids. Dehydration can make headaches, fatigue, and a sore throat feel worse.
- **Worse sleep.** Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster but tends to disrupt sleep later in the night. Good sleep is one of the few things that reliably helps you recover from a cold.
- **Immune effects.** Heavy drinking is well known to weaken the immune system over time, and studies of binge drinking in healthy volunteers have found short-term changes in immune cell activity within hours. Whether one or two drinks meaningfully slows recovery from a cold hasn't been well studied, but there's no evidence alcohol helps.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and being sick often means you're eating less, which is also bad news for your liver's acetaminophen clean-up system.

"A hot toddy" is a traditional cold remedy, and the warm liquid, honey, and lemon may soothe a sore throat. The whiskey is the part with no evidence behind it, and it's the part that doesn't mix with DayQuil.

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining DayQuil and alcohol, or before using DayQuil at all, if any of these apply to you:

- You drink 3 or more alcoholic drinks most days.
- You have liver disease, hepatitis, or have been told your liver enzymes are high.
- You have high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, or diabetes, or trouble urinating due to an enlarged prostate (the label lists these for the decongestant).
- You take an MAOI, or any antidepressant, or other prescription medicines.
- You take blood thinners such as warfarin, since regular acetaminophen use can affect them.
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding.
- You're an older adult, or you're giving cold medicine to a teenager or child. Check the label for age-specific dosing.

For a wider look at how alcohol and common supplements interact with prescription and over-the-counter medicines, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs That Need Medical Attention

Get help right away by calling Poison Control (**1-800-222-1222** in the US) or 911 in an emergency if you notice any of the following after combining DayQuil and alcohol, or after taking more DayQuil than the label allows:

- **Possible acetaminophen overdose:** nausea, vomiting, sweating, loss of appetite, or just feeling unwell in the first day. These can look like a hangover or the flu, which is exactly why they're easy to miss. Later signs include pain under the right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, unusual bruising, or confusion. Don't wait for symptoms. The hospital antidote (N-acetylcysteine, or NAC) works best when given early.
- **Too much dextromethorphan or too much sedation:** severe dizziness, confusion, hallucinations, agitation, extreme sleepiness, or slow or shallow breathing.
- **Heart or blood pressure problems:** chest pain, a racing or pounding heartbeat, a severe headache, or fainting.
- **Possible serotonin syndrome** (mainly in people on antidepressants): agitation, fever, sweating, muscle twitching or stiffness, and a fast heart rate.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

People land on this page for two reasons: they're sick and wondering if a drink is OK, or they drink and want to protect their liver. For the first group, the answer is above: skip the drink or keep it to a minimum and time it away from DayQuil.

For the second group, the most effective liver protection is the unglamorous one: drink less, drink more slowly, eat, and hydrate. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. To be clear about its limits:

- Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, not proven.
- **There's no evidence DHM protects against acetaminophen liver damage**, and it doesn't make it safe to combine DayQuil, Tylenol, or any acetaminophen product with alcohol.
- Like any supplement, it can interact with medicines. If you take prescription drugs, check with a pharmacist first.

If you want to try it on nights you drink (not while sick and taking cold medicine), popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly.

## The Bottom Line

DayQuil doesn't contain alcohol, but it doesn't mix well with it either. The acetaminophen is the ingredient that matters most: it shares the liver's workload with alcohol, and the real danger comes from heavy regular drinking, exceeding the label dose, or doubling up with Tylenol, NyQuil, or other cold products. Dextromethorphan adds dizziness and drowsiness, and it can be dangerous with certain antidepressants or at high doses. Phenylephrine's interaction with alcohol is modest, and the FDA's advisers have concluded it doesn't work well as a decongestant anyway.

The simplest safe plan is to skip alcohol while you're sick and taking DayQuil. If you do drink, space it well away from your doses, keep it light, never add extra acetaminophen, and ask a pharmacist or doctor if you drink regularly or take other medicines.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking DayQuil?**

It's best not to. DayQuil contains acetaminophen, which shares the liver's workload with alcohol, plus dextromethorphan, which can add to alcohol's dizziness and drowsiness. A single drink with a single labeled dose is unlikely to cause serious harm in a healthy adult, but the label warns against using it if you have 3 or more drinks every day, and being sick is a poor time to drink anyway.

**Does DayQuil have alcohol in it?**

No. The standard DayQuil Cold & Flu liquid and LiquiCaps don't list alcohol as an ingredient. You may be thinking of NyQuil: the original NyQuil liquid lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient, though alcohol-free NyQuil versions exist. Formulas vary, so check the inactive ingredients on your package if avoiding alcohol completely matters to you.

**How long after taking DayQuil can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting time. DayQuil is dosed every 4 hours, so a cautious approach is to wait at least until that window has passed, ideally longer, and keep it to one drink. Dextromethorphan can last much longer in people who break it down slowly. If you drink 3 or more drinks a day regularly, ask a doctor before using DayQuil at all.

**Can I take DayQuil for a hangover?**

It's not a good idea. DayQuil is made for cold and flu symptoms, not hangovers, and the morning after heavy drinking is a poor time to give your liver acetaminophen, especially on an empty stomach. If you take it anyway, wait until the alcohol has cleared, eat first, take one standard dose, and never add Tylenol on top.

**Can I take Tylenol and DayQuil together?**

No, not without a doctor's advice. Both contain acetaminophen, and taking them together is one of the most common ways people accidentally go over the daily limit. The same applies to taking DayQuil and NyQuil close together, since standard NyQuil also contains acetaminophen. Count acetaminophen from every product you take.

**Is DayQuil or NyQuil worse with alcohol?**

NyQuil is generally the riskier combination. It contains doxylamine, a sedating antihistamine that adds to alcohol's sedation and can cause heavy drowsiness and, in larger amounts, slowed breathing. Both products contain acetaminophen, so both share the liver concern.

**What happens if you accidentally mix DayQuil and alcohol?**

If you took one labeled dose and had a drink or two, the most likely result is feeling more dizzy or tired than usual. Don't take another dose until the alcohol has cleared, drink water, and avoid driving. If you took more than the labeled dose, drink heavily on a regular basis, or feel nauseous, confused, or unwell, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) right away.

**Does DHM make it safe to take DayQuil with alcohol?**

No. There's no evidence that DHM protects against acetaminophen liver damage, and it doesn't change the label's warnings. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. Follow the DayQuil label and talk to a pharmacist if you're unsure.
